Potentiometers / Technical reference

Audio vs Linear Taper Pots

Separate the resistance curve from the control’s in-circuit response, and choose a useful sweep for volume or tone.

Published 4 October 2026

In this guide
  1. Resistance and taper answer different questions
  2. Why audio taper is common for volume
  3. Tone-control sweep is a circuit result
  4. Measure the curve, not just the label
  5. Treble bleeds can change the sweep too
  6. A useful specification
  7. Next steps

Resistance and taper answer different questions

A pot’s nominal resistance is measured between the ends of the complete track. Taper describes the proportion of that resistance between the wiper and each end as the shaft rotates. A 500 kΩ linear pot and a 500 kΩ audio pot can therefore measure similarly end to end while producing different wiper readings halfway through their travel.

For an approximately linear track, halfway rotation gives approximately half the full resistance on each side of the wiper. An audio or logarithmic track deliberately uses a different curve. Real audio tapers can be segmented approximations and come in different proportions; the word audio does not specify one universal transfer curve. Read the manufacturer’s drawing or curve when the sweep matters.

Why audio taper is common for volume

Perceived loudness does not follow voltage in a simple linear way. An audio taper is commonly chosen to make volume adjustment more useful across the rotation range. That is a design convention, not proof that the knob position is a calibrated loudness control. Pickup impedance, the load and any bypass network affect the electrical response, while amplification and listening conditions affect what a player hears.

A linear pot can still be useful for volume when its adjustment range suits the player and circuit. The question is where the useful changes occur. If most of the audible change seems crowded into a small part of the travel, compare the actual taper and connected network before blaming the resistance value. Do not expect a different printed taper label to remove every interaction.

Tone-control sweep is a circuit result

A conventional tone control varies resistance in a capacitor loading branch. It does not use the pot as exactly the same voltage divider as the volume circuit. Its frequency-dependent behaviour means that the resistance-versus-rotation curve and the pickup/load response both determine how the control feels.

Audio and linear tapers are both used for tone controls. One may give a more useful range in a particular instrument, but there is no rule that the component marked audio must be used for volume and the component marked linear must be used for tone. Compare the intended tone network and the player’s useful settings, including the region near the fully rolled-down position.

Measure the curve, not just the label

Bench checks with an isolated pot
MeasurementWhat it tells you
End terminal to end terminalActual full-track resistance
Wiper to each end at half travelAn approximate midpoint taper ratio
Wiper readings through the travelDirection, continuity and the shape of the sweep

The direction matters. Turning clockwise in the installed orientation should produce the intended change; swapping the end functions changes the direction of the resistance sweep. A reversed audio taper is not equivalent to an ordinary audio taper installed backwards if the useful curve needs to run in the other direction.

Letter codes vary

Do not infer audio or linear solely from an A or B printed on a casing without checking that manufacturer’s coding convention. Use the datasheet and measurement.

Treble bleeds can change the sweep too

A capacitor between volume input and wiper adds a frequency-dependent bypass path. A resistor associated with it also changes how the network behaves, so a treble bleed can alter the apparent volume progression as well as the high-frequency balance. The original pot taper remains a component property, but the complete control response has changed.

Compare at the same knob position and also at matched practical output levels. Those comparisons answer different questions. An electrical model can show the effect of stated assumptions; it does not model perceived loudness. Use the Treble Bleed Designer to explore the network without treating its curve as a guaranteed listening result.

A useful specification

Record nominal resistance, actual tolerance, taper family or curve, rotation direction and mounting requirements. If you like the existing sweep, replace like for like rather than changing taper incidentally during a repair. If the sweep is the problem, keep resistance and the surrounding circuit consistent while trying a different curve.

Mechanical quality, contact reliability and fit remain important. A premium label does not replace a taper specification. The best choice for the job is a control whose usable range, electrical load and physical dimensions are appropriate for the instrument.

Understand. Experiment. Build.
